paras: The killing of James Hamilton at Mill Springs was the shooting of Hamilton and the wounding and capture of Jesse Myers by a search party under Capt. W. T. Leeper near Mill Springs, Wayne County, Missouri, at daybreak on May 21, 1881. The men were wanted for shooting the county's sheriff and collector the day before; a third, Frank Brown, surrendered that evening. Threats to lynch Myers and Brown led the New Madrid County sheriff to remove them to St. Louis, and both were later convicted and hanged.

According to a New Madrid County reward circular printed in Wheeling, the band attacked William Knox's house on May 9, fatally wounding a girl, and on May 11 killed posseman Robert Laforge near Bayne's store. A fourth member, Robert Rhodes, surrendered wounded and died; the Memphis Public Ledger said he was "taken out and hung by the citizens." On Friday, May 20, by the Iron County Register's account, Sheriff John T. Davis and Collector James F. Hatton confronted two strangers at a house near Greenville, and both officials were shot. Five hundred men then took to the woods, and rewards totalled $4,000.

Leeper, "an old and substantial citizen of Wayne county," posted a party overnight at Campbell's Switch, a ferry crossing on Black River two miles below Mill Springs. At first light Myers and Hamilton walked up the railroad, and Leeper cocked his gun and called, "Hold on there." In the posse's account the men "wheeled and presented their shot-guns" and the party fired at the same moment; the People's Vindicator said both were shot after "refusing to surrender."

Hamilton was killed by buckshot in the head and Myers fell with a forehead wound; both were carried by hand-car to Mill Springs, where Hamilton was buried. Brown was tracked into Reynolds County and at dusk surrendered without resistance to a party including Prosecuting Attorney J. N. Morrison.

The first wire reported that "threats of lynching have been made," and the Public Ledger said the wives of Myers and Hamilton were put under guard. After the prisoners reached the New Madrid jail on May 22, Sheriff R. J. Walters, fearing a lynching, slipped them across the river to Hickman, Kentucky, and on Governor Crittenden's instruction took them to the St. Louis jail. The Register wrote that "three hundred citizens were on the alert" for a lynching that Sunday night.

Brown and Myers were convicted of murder in June, and a third prisoner, Theo. Mitchell, pleaded guilty and received thirty years. The two were hanged at New Madrid on July 15 before a crowd the Memphis Daily Appeal put at "fully 5000." No report of an inquest on Hamilton appears in the coverage.

Most papers ran a St. Louis wire of May 21 under headlines such as "Western Outlaws Captured" (Wheeling Daily Intelligencer) and "Desperadoes Disposed of" (Memphis Daily Appeal). All accounts called the men "outlaws" or "desperadoes" and told the shooting from the posse's side; the Register called them "the hunted game." The Public Ledger quoted the Lake County Star that "such outlaws ought to be executed in the latest style of the art as soon as caught up with," and agreed.

The Wheeling paper took a local angle under the headline "Is It Our Jesse," reporting that Myers was from West Virginia and Hamilton from Shelbyville, Illinois. The Appeal headed the execution "Hanging of a Couple of Cut-Throats ... Not a Whit Too Soon." No report gives the race of any of the men.

The Chicago Tribune dated the capture "last Friday" and the Crawford Avalanche placed it "near Piedmont," against the Saturday, Mill Springs account of the wire and the local Register. The wire called Myers "mortally wounded," the Register "only temporarily stunned"; he lived to be hanged. Davis was first reported killed, then "perhaps mortally wounded"; the Register said he died Sunday morning.

bases: A citizens' search party under Capt. W. T. Leeper shot and killed Hamilton and wounded Myers while trying to take them at Campbell's Switch, and threats to lynch the surviving prisoners followed (A4, A10, A13).

The St. Louis wire (A4), the local Iron County Register (A10), the New Madrid Record synopsis (A19) and a later Wheeling report (A13) agree that Leeper's party killed Hamilton and captured Myers near Mill Springs.

accounts.label: New Madrid Record synopsis

framing.detail: Most dailies ran the May 21 wire under heads such as 'Western Outlaws Captured' and 'Desperadoes Disposed of', calling the men 'outlaws'.
The Iron County Register called the men 'the hunted game' and the posse 'faithful guards', and gave the posse's account without question.
The Memphis Public Ledger quoted the Lake County Star that such outlaws 'ought to be executed in the latest style of the art as soon as caught up with' and agreed.
The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer took a local angle, 'Is It Our Jesse', on Myers's past in Wheeling.
The Memphis Daily Appeal headed the legal hanging 'Hanging of a Couple of Cut-Throats ... Not a Whit Too Soon'.

info: Saturday, May 21, 1881, at daybreak (wire and local paper); the Chicago Tribune says the men were captured 'last Friday' (May 20).
Campbell's Switch, a ferry crossing on Black River about two miles below Mill Springs; one summary says 'near Piedmont'.
James Hamilton (killed); Jesse Myers or Meyers (wounded, captured); Frank Brown (surrendered later the same day to another party). Race not stated for any of them.

Accused of shooting Sheriff John T. Davis and Collector James F. Hatton near Greenville the day before, and of an earlier attack on William Knox's house and the killing of posseman Robert Laforge in New Madrid County.
A search party under Capt. W. T. Leeper, 'an old and substantial citizen of Wayne county', who had consulted Ambrose Beatty, Cal. Thomas and Taylor Fulton.
Brown and Myers hanged at New Madrid, July 15, 1881, before about 5,000 people. Hamilton buried at Mill Spring.
